title: Linkability of GPS Location Data
description: Continuous GPS position data captured by the wearable device can be linked across time periods to reconstruct the user's movement patterns, daily routines, and frequent locations, potentially revealing sensitive information about the user's life.
assumptions: GPS data is transmitted or stored in a way that preserves location precision over time

title: Identification via Sensor Telemetry
description: The combination of heart rate, step counts, GPS position, and timestamps can uniquely identify the user, especially when correlated with known activities or locations. This creates a persistent identifier that could be used to track the individual.
assumptions: Sensor data is accessible to unauthorized parties or stored in identifiable format

title: Disclosure of Sensitive Health and Location Data
description: Heart rate and continuous sensor telemetry constitute sensitive health information. If the wearable device data is transmitted, stored, or accessed by unauthorized parties, this could lead to privacy violations and potential misuse of health data.
assumptions: Data transmission or storage lacks adequate encryption or access controls

title: Excessive Data Collection via Continuous Monitoring
description: Continuous capture of sensor telemetry (heart rate, step counts, GPS, timestamps) may exceed what is necessary for the device's intended function, violating data minimization principles. Users may be collecting more data than required for basic fitness tracking.
assumptions: The device operates in continuous monitoring mode by default without user opt-in for each data type

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Companion App
description: Wearable device (P1) explicitly transfers personal data (GPS traces, device id, timestamps, exercise sessions) to companion mobile app (P2) by design. This represents an intentional data disclosure across a process boundary.
assumptions: The wearable device has no local storage capability or the data must be processed by the companion app for functionality.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context [4] on data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Potential Over-collection of Personal Data
description: The flow transfers GPS traces and device id which may exceed minimality principle requirements. Continuous GPS tracking and device identifiers could be collected beyond what's strictly necessary for exercise session tracking.
assumptions: Companion app may use this data for purposes beyond the stated exercise session tracking.
uncertainty_note: Assumes app functionality requirements not fully specified.

title: Data Disclosure from App to Third Parties
description: Companion mobile app (P2) may further disclose the received personal data (GPS traces, device id, timestamps) to external third parties (e.g., cloud services, analytics providers, advertisers) beyond the wearable device's intended scope.
assumptions: App may have integrations with external services not modeled in this DFD.
uncertainty_note: External data flows not shown in this DFD; threat is consequential based on typical app behavior.

title: Unawareness of Health Data Usage
description: The user may not be fully aware of how their calorie, meal, and weight data is being used, shared, or stored beyond the app's stated purpose. Mobile apps often collect health data for purposes beyond the primary function.
assumptions: User has not reviewed privacy policy thoroughly; app may share data with third parties
uncertainty_note: Using tree node U.1.2 from context as it relates to unawareness of personal data sharing

title: Linkability of Health Data to Other Sources
description: The user's health data (calories, meals, weight) could be linked to other data sources (e.g., location data, purchase history, other apps) to create a comprehensive profile of the user's lifestyle and health status.
assumptions: Data may be shared with third-party services or integrated with other platforms

title: Identifiability from Health Data Patterns
description: The combination of weight entries, meal logs, and calorie intake data could potentially identify the user, especially when combined with other data sources or metadata (e.g., timestamps, device information).
assumptions: Health data patterns are relatively unique to individuals; data may be combined with other identifiers

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Sensitive Health Data
description: There is a risk that sensitive health data (weight, meal logs, calorie intake) could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through vulnerabilities in the app, insecure data transmission, or improper access controls.
assumptions: Mobile apps are common targets for security breaches; data may be stored on servers with inadequate protection

title: Explicit Health Data Disclosure to Health Log Store
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) explicitly transfers personal health data (calorie intake, weight history, exercise sessions) to the Health Log Store (DS1) as part of its designed functionality. This represents an explicit data disclosure where personal data crosses a system boundary.
assumptions: The health log store is a separate system from the mobile app, and the data transfer is intentional and by design.

title: Health Log Data Identifiability Risk
description: Health logs containing calorie intake, weight history, and exercise sessions are inherently personal data that can identify individuals. When stored in DS1, this data remains identifiable and could be used to profile users.
assumptions: Health data is considered personal data under privacy regulations, and the data in DS1 is not sufficiently anonymized.

title: Unauthorized Access to Health Log Store
description: The Health Log Store (DS1) containing sensitive health data may be accessible to unauthorized parties. Without proper access controls, malicious actors could potentially access or exfiltrate the stored health logs.
assumptions: The health log store has network exposure or insufficient access controls.

title: Health Log Data Integrity Risk
description: Health logs stored in DS1 could be altered, corrupted, or tampered with by unauthorized actors or system failures, compromising the accuracy and reliability of the health data.
assumptions: The health log store lacks adequate integrity controls or audit mechanisms.

title: Explicit Location Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: The Companion Mobile App writes GPS location traces with timestamps to the Location History Store. If the store is accessible to third parties (e.g., cloud service, analytics provider, or law enforcement), this constitutes explicit data disclosure of highly sensitive personal data. Location data reveals movement patterns, home/work locations, and daily routines.
assumptions: The Location History Store may be accessible to entities beyond the immediate app owner or user consent scope.
uncertainty_note: Assuming the store architecture allows third-party access; would need to verify actual access controls.

title: Linkability of Location Traces to User Identity
description: GPS location traces with timestamps can be linked to identify a specific user's movements and patterns. Even if anonymized, the combination of location data and timestamps creates a unique movement profile that can be correlated with other data sources to re-identify individuals.
assumptions: Location data is stored in a format that allows correlation across time periods or with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Assuming the data is stored in a way that enables linking; depends on actual storage and access mechanisms.

title: Identifiability of User from Location Data
description: GPS location data is inherently identifiable as it tracks the physical movements of a specific device/user. The combination of location coordinates and timestamps can uniquely identify an individual's presence at specific places and times, violating privacy expectations.
assumptions: The location data is not properly pseudonymized or anonymized before storage.
uncertainty_note: Assuming no additional anonymization measures are applied; depends on actual data processing pipeline.

title: Location Data Integrity Compromise
description: GPS location traces stored in the Location History Store could be altered, deleted, or tampered with without detection. This could lead to inaccurate location history, denial of service, or manipulation of location-based services.
assumptions: The data store lacks adequate integrity controls (e.g., cryptographic signatures, audit logs).
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard storage without specialized integrity mechanisms; would need to verify actual security controls.

title: Implicit Health Data Disclosure via Analytics Processing
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise patterns) is read by the analytics service for health-condition analysis. This represents implicit disclosure where personal health data is transferred across the DataStore-Process boundary. The minimality principle may be violated if the analytics service accesses more data than strictly required for the stated health-condition analysis purpose.
assumptions: The analytics service has access to historical health logs across multiple sessions, creating a comprehensive health profile that could be disclosed beyond intended scope.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [3] and [5] - this is a reasonable fit for DataStore→Process data disclosure

title: Linkability of Health Log Patterns to Individual
description: Calorie, weight, and exercise logs across multiple sessions can be linked to identify specific individuals' health behaviors and patterns. The combination of data points creates a unique health profile that could be linked to other data sources or used to re-identify anonymized data.
assumptions: Health log data contains sufficient granularity and temporal patterns to enable linking across sessions and potentially to other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a standard linkability node - health data inherently carries linkability risk

title: Identifiability Through Health Pattern Analysis
description: The analytics service processes health logs that could be used to identify individuals through health-condition analysis. Even if direct identifiers are removed, the combination of weight, exercise, and calorie data across sessions may enable indirect identification through health pattern matching.
assumptions: Health patterns are sufficiently unique to enable identification, especially when combined with other data sources.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a standard identifiability node - health data is inherently identifiable

title: Data Integrity Risk in Health Analytics Processing
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) processes health log data and could potentially alter, corrupt, or tamper with the calorie, weight, and exercise records during analysis. This could lead to inaccurate health-condition analysis and potentially harmful medical decisions based on compromised data.
assumptions: The analytics service has write or modify capabilities, or data could be corrupted during processing/transmission.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a standard integrity node - integrity risk exists for any data processing operation

title: Non-compliance with Health Data Privacy Regulations
description: The health analytics service may not comply with applicable privacy regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR) regarding health data processing. Processing calorie, weight, and exercise logs for health-condition analysis may require specific consent, data minimization, and security measures that are not guaranteed.
assumptions: Health data is subject to regulatory requirements, and the analytics service may not have proper compliance controls in place.
uncertainty_note: Using Nc.1.1 as a standard non-compliance node - health data processing typically has regulatory implications

title: Explicit Location Data Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: Location history data is explicitly transferred from the Location History Store to the Health Analytics Service for pattern analysis. This disclosure is by design but raises concerns about data minimality - the system may be collecting and sharing more location data than strictly necessary for the intended health analytics purpose.
assumptions: The analytics service has access to full location history across multiple sessions, enabling derivation of daily routines and movement patterns.

title: Linkability of Location History Across Sessions
description: Location history data stored in DS2 may be linkable across different sessions, potentially revealing the user's complete movement patterns and daily routines. This could enable profiling beyond the intended health analytics scope.
assumptions: Location data is retained across multiple sessions and can be correlated to build comprehensive movement profiles.

title: Identifiability Through Location Patterns
description: Location history data may be identifiable and traceable to specific individuals, especially when combined with the derived daily routine and movement patterns. Unique location signatures could enable re-identification even with anonymization attempts.
assumptions: Location patterns are unique to individuals and can be used to identify users even without direct identifiers.

title: Profiling via Health Analytics Insights
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) processes health data to generate inferred insights (risk indicators, routine summaries, trend flags) that could enable profiling of individuals or groups. When these insights are returned to the Companion Mobile App (P2), they may reveal patterns about health conditions that could be used to profile individuals or infer characteristics about groups of similar individuals.
assumptions: The analytics service aggregates or processes data from multiple users, and the inferred insights contain enough information to enable meaningful profiling.
uncertainty_note: Using L.2.2.2 from retrieved context; the exact profiling capability depends on the granularity of the inferred insights.

title: Insufficient cybersecurity risk management for health data transmission
description: The transmission of health analytics data from the Health Analytics Service (P3) to the Companion Mobile App (P2) may lack adequate cybersecurity risk management controls. Given the sensitive nature of health data, insufficient encryption, authentication, or access controls could lead to privacy breaches and regulatory non-compliance (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR).
assumptions: Health data is considered sensitive/protected information requiring strict cybersecurity and privacy compliance measures.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 from retrieved context; actual compliance status depends on organizational security practices not visible in the DFD.

title: Identity inference from health insights
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) receives inferred health insights that could potentially allow identification of the data subject through correlation with other known information. Even if data is anonymized at the service level, the app may have access to additional context that enables re-identification.
assumptions: The app has access to user identity information that could be correlated with the health insights received.
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN node; the actual risk depends on what identity information the app possesses.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health condition indicators
description: The app displays sensitive health condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the user. If the app has vulnerabilities or if the user shares this information with third parties, the data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties beyond the intended recipient.
assumptions: The app may have security vulnerabilities; users may share health information with others
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as a reasonable node for data disclosure in Process→ExternalEntity flow
